"Diagnosing lung infections using computed tomography (CT) scans is a prevalent and vital task in clinical practice. While Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have demonstrated effectiveness in analyzing lung CT imagery for disease detection, their performance is often constrained by the limitations of standard, pre-trained CNN architectures. To overcome this, we introduce a new diagnostic framework for identifying COVID-19 from lung CT scans that utilizes Vision Transformers (VTs), cutting-edge models capable of long-range spatial modeling. Specifically, we employ two VT architectures, Swin Transformer and Vision Transformer (ViT), to replace conventional pre-trained CNNs for extracting image features. These models are fine-tuned using a dataset of approximately 1,000 COVID-19 chest CT scans balanced with an equal number of normal scans. To further enhance performance, we assess two fine-tuning strategies: fine-tuning the entire model versus fine-tuning only the initial layers. Our experimental results demonstrate that fine-tuning the entire model outperforms tuning only the first layers. Furthermore, fine-tuned Swin Transformer and ViT configurations achieve superior performance compared to fine-tuned ResNet50 models. The final evaluation shows that our proposed framework reaches a mean accuracy of 96.2% and a mean F1-score of 96.1%."

Network science is a rapidly expanding and evolving field characterized by complex systems and their mathematical models. It is a highly interdisciplinary pursuit drawing from mathematics, physics, computer science, and beyond. While the majority of existing network research has concentrated on the structure of networks, there has been a growing interest in the dynamics that occur upon them. This document provides a comprehensive overview of network science, covering topics ranging from the various types of networks to the statistical and mathematical frameworks used for their analysis, as well as the exploration of both structure and dynamics.

While eco-evolutionary feedbacks and the acceleration of global change define the core issues in this field, a comprehensive framework for addressing these challenges is currently missing. This article introduces a structured research agenda to advance these interdisciplines, leveraging established and emerging mathematical techniques. Our plan prioritizes four key areas: (1) clarifying the consequences on timescales relevant to contemporary global shifts, (2) defining the criteria under which evolution exerts timely impacts within a changing world, (3) quantifying the influence of eco-evolutionary processes in fluctuating environments, and (4) developing robust, generalizable models that remain accurate despite simplifying assumptions. We further examine critical obstacles hindering progress in the field and outline essential future research directions.

This work introduces a comprehensive evaluation of self-supervised learning (SSL) for speech using the Speech Bank Benchmark, a new framework designed to simplify and streamline the assessment of self-supervised methods across diverse downstream tasks. Through Speech Bank, we present results from leading state-of-the-art models spanning four different training paradigms. Our analysis reveals that while these learning strategies offer distinct advantages and applications, they collectively achieve significant performance gains over traditional supervised baselines. Notably, the most advanced models reduce error rates in speech recognition by 30% and improve speaker identification accuracy by 40% while utilizing only 2% of available data.

Automated Market Makers (AMMs) serve as the dominant method for peer-to-peer crypto asset trading. In AMMs, Liquidity Providers (LPs) establish prices via an exchange algorithm, while Exchange Users execute trades against LP asset reserves. Price fluctuations, particularly in volatile markets, significantly impact LPs' portfolio values. This study isolates an LP's financial outcome by abstracting market price mechanics into a single Price Curve, which aggregates exchange activity and exchange rule systems. Through this lens, we analyze an LP's profit or loss relative to their initial investment and starting portfolio composition. Our findings indicate a universal characteristic: in most AMM architectures, profit or loss scales with trade volume and portfolio volatility. Furthermore, a threshold effect exists where LP gains or losses become negligible only when trade size is sufficiently small. These results offer a concise framework for evaluating LP outcomes, assisting LPs in making informed decisions regarding participation and helping Exchange Users understand the cost implications of their trades.

Sensitivity Analysis serves as a framework for evaluating how conclusions depend on unobserved (missing) outcome data, a method that is increasingly prevalent in clinical trials. This article introduces SAS implementations of the X-to-P model and its extensions, which are widely utilized in sensitivity analysis. These implementations include code for experiment-specific parameters, allowing users to conduct experiment-independent analyses via Generalized Linear Models. Furthermore, the author provides graphical R tools to visualize sensitivity analysis results and demonstrates their integration with SAS for end-to-end analysis. This approach facilitates graph generation directly within SAS using macro-driven code, which can then be exported using standard file transfer capabilities. Finally, the article concludes with a practical example illustrating the complete workflow, from data input in R and MCMC simulation in R to result visualization in R, all orchestrated by controlling functions in R.

This study examines $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries defined on jet spaces within noncommutative differential calculus for a commutative algebra, focusing on the fourth quantum Weyl algebra. By analyzing the action of the Cartan generator's representation on this calculus, we derive specific forms for the raised and lowered ladder operators. Leveraging these operators and existing research, we characterize integral functions in the quantum algebra and construct invariant functions across diverse quantum jet spaces. Furthermore, the analysis characterizes the quantum differential jet as a quantum principal bundle and identifies the quantum velocity jet as a quantum subbundle. Finally, the study outlines conditions for both invariant and non-invariant vector fields within these jet frameworks.

The rise of intelligent vehicles has spurred significant research into advanced technologies like federated learning (FL) and blockchain. FL is particularly well-suited for IoT vehicles, offering robust data privacy, security, and the ability to scale effectively. Conversely, blockchain excels at providing trustless, transparent, and verifiable data storage. This study proposes a combined blockchain-enhanced federated learning (BEFL) framework for the Internet of Vehicles. In this model, vehicles participate in the learning process by sending only their local model updates to the edge server, thereby safeguarding data privacy. Additionally, the integration of blockchain facilitates the secure exchange of these updates and enables efficient, low-cost consensus for network management tasks such as monitoring and routing. The proposed system is validated through a real-world simulation using a vehicle dataset from the UCI Machine Learning Repository. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed BEFL method outperforms traditional FL approaches in terms of training efficiency and effectiveness.

The ALICE Collaboration investigates the production cross sections for $J/\psi$, $\psi(2S)$, and their daughter leptons in proton-proton and $^{3}$He–proton collisions at the LHC's LHC, utilizing data from 2010 to 2015. Reconstructing these heavy mesons via decays into $e^+e^-$ pairs, the study employs an extended maximum likelihood fit to determine yields. By comparing yields to a baseline, normalized cross sections are derived and subsequently converted into absolute values using integrated luminosity measurements. Measurements span transverse momentum ranges of $p_T < 6$ GeV/$c$ for $J/\psi$ and $p_T < 3$ GeV/$c$ for $\psi(2S)$, with pseudorapidity coverage of $2.9 < |\eta| < 2.4$. Additionally, polarization is assessed in the $J$ plane relative to its production plane. A distinct ALICE trigger, designed to enhance $J$ and $J$ signal detection, is analyzed and found to contribute significantly to both samples.

Achieving millikelvin temperatures using new cryogenic cooling infrastructure is essential for scaling the number of qubits in various quantum computing approaches. This study introduces a customized pulse-tube-based dilution refrigerator featuring a base temperature of 75 mK, designed to support up to 16 wires, with performance validated through silicon-based microwave resonators. Additionally, we present preliminary findings on a high-temperature superconducting NbTiN planar resonator, whose measured total loss characteristics are analyzed in relation to its intrinsic surface loss parameters.

Cryptocurrencies have become a primary target for cybercriminals, prompting the migration of funds to the blockchain. To ensure the integrity of these transactions, security is paramount; however, flaws within crypto protocols and applications frequently expose users to significant risks. Consequently, researchers have been investigating crypto misapplications to educate developers and promote sound coding practices. This study presents a large-scale empirical analysis examining API misuse across 1,000 GitHub-hosted Python projects. Our findings reveal that 22% of analyzed projects contained crypto API misuses, with the majority involving 256 encryption schemes, hashes, digital signatures, and the encryption block cipher mode of operation (CBC). Furthermore, 43% of projects utilized insecure random number generators. A key observation is that while many projects contained errors, the same mistakes were often repeated across multiple projects. To combat this pattern of duplication, we propose the use of machine learning to develop a scalable and efficient detection system.

We introduce a new method for sparse signal deconvolution that is particularly well-suited to seismic reflectivity inversion. This method reformulates deconvolution as an optimization task involving an objective composed of a data-fidelity term and a regularization term based on a wavelet transform of the sparse coefficients. We propose a simplified iterative algorithm capable of handling general wavelets. Its performance on synthetic seismic models demonstrates that the method effectively produces sparse outputs even from noisy inputs with non-uniform sampling, while maintaining sparsity in cases where the true reflectivity sequence was initially undersampled. These findings indicate that our approach could become a valuable tool for modern seismic reflectivity inversion.

Operator product expansion (OPE) coefficients are fundamental to conformal field theories (CFTs), yet direct measurement remains elusive for quantum field theories (QFTs) due to the complexity of isolating individual operator products of distance-dependent correlators. This work introduces OPE coefficients defined at the energy scale $\mu$ within the operator product expansion framework of renormalization group (RG) flow. Our approach introduces a novel method grounded in the renormalization scheme for extracting these coefficients, bypassing the need for separate OPE data by utilizing existing RG flow information such as anomalous dimensions and RG eigenoperators. By applying this framework to $\phi^4$ theory in four dimensions, we derive constraints on the scale-dependent OPE coefficients for the relevant operators and use numerical RG techniques to validate the results.

Assigning part-of-speech (POS) tags to historical texts is a difficult task, complicated by the presence of morphological complexity and a scarcity of suitable training data. This study introduces a strategy for historical POS tagging that draws on morphological features and unsupervised, large-scale pre-trained language models. Our method employs a sparse bi-encoder architecture, which streamlines the integration of both unsupervised model outputs and domain-specific features. The system is designed to operate as a single forward pass, thereby reducing the need for time-intensive unsupervised inference. Furthermore, our approach can function as a zero-shot model or be fine-tuned using a small amount of labeled data. Experimental findings indicate that this method achieves state-of-the-art performance in zero-shot scenarios across three distinct Indo-European languages, while fine-tuned results are competitive with deep contextual models that demand significantly more training data.

This study examines a monopolist who attempts to implement a demand function through direct revelation mechanisms. Since mechanisms can only be constructed from validated demand functions, the research establishes the necessary and sufficient conditions for a candidate function to qualify. The core condition equates the monotonicity of the function with both the boundedness and continuity of its derivative. Building on this, the study presents a spectrum of strategies that enable any valid demand function to be realized by direct revelation mechanisms involving transfer payments. These methods are then applied to determine optimal implementations for regular regularization functions and explore additional applications involving continuum bidding agents.

Intelligent assistant systems, exemplified by CitySpec, are designed to help city stakeholders achieve their objectives through interactive data-driven visualizations. These tools, however, often overwhelm users with excessive information, making it difficult to quickly identify relevant data relevant to their specific tasks. To address this challenge, we introduce a data-driven approach for automatically identifying the most pertinent information based on user queries and presenting it via an interactive, focused visualization. Our solution integrates three core components: a keyword expansion module that enriches input with synonyms using WordNet; a ranking system that leverages the expanded keywords to score data records; and a filtering mechanism that isolates and displays only the top-ranked records. We evaluated this method on a real-world city traffic dataset and confirmed its effectiveness through user studies.

We introduce a method for error mitigation that leverages hidden inverses to correct circuits without explicit optimization. These inverses, which do not need to be explicitly identified or implemented, are used to calculate post-selection on specific output states derived from circuits combined with their respective inverses. Error rates are then estimated using noise parameters. Validation is performed using multiple simulation methods, including the quantum Monte Carlo technique, to address both coherent and incoherent errors. This method can achieve significant improvements in the fidelity of single- and multi-qubit circuits, particularly when error probabilities are moderate.

In any regular category $\mathcal{Q}$, the direct image of a preorder via a morphism $f$ results in another preorder; specifically, the collection of subpreorders within $\mathcal{Q}$ constitutes a poset denoted as $\mathsf{SubPre}(f)$. We establish that $f$ maps the cocartesian image of a set of subpreorders to their supremum inside $\mathcal{Q}$. Consequently, the cocartesian operation factors through the poset $\mathsf{SubPre}(f)$ to yield a supremum. This theorem is applied to the category $\mathsf{Rel}$, which comprises binary relations, and to any regular category $\mathcal{Q}$. In these contexts, the cocartesian image of a set of subpreorders corresponds to the supremum of all individual subpreorders. This equivalence holds without necessitating a specific existence of true suprema within $\mathcal{Q}$. Furthermore, the discussion addresses scenarios where regular epi-mono factorizations utilize constructive methods, highlighting that the formulation remains valid in a constructive framework.

Recently, Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) has been widely adopted for few-shot learning due to its ability to acquire generalizable visual and textual representations. Nevertheless, its text-image pre-training objective primarily optimizes alignment, often causing a downstream task optimum to be overlooked. To address this, we introduce Gated Multi-Projection (GMP), an approach that employs a gating mechanism alongside multiple projection layers to dynamically select the most suitable projection for specific tasks. Empirical evaluations on six recognition tasks—including general object detection and specialized domains like medical imagery—demonstrate that GMP consistently enhances CLIP's performance. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights and practical evidence confirming that multiple projection layers are essential for achieving these gains.

Machine learning has become a vital tool for medical image analysis, yet this progress is hindered by fragmented repositories that fail to offer efficient access to imaging datasets. DICOM, the industry standard for medical image interchange, is the format utilized by virtually all machine learning collections in this field. Nevertheless, many datasets remain hosted in incompatible proprietary formats, necessitating manual conversion efforts that are time-consuming and error-prone. We introduce a streamlined pipeline for training medical image datasets in the standard DICOM format. Our solution utilizes PyTorch-Gan's version-control capabilities to manage data flow and integrates Minz (Zonal-Dependent Compression in Medical InsidZonal? Minz is a zonal-dependent compression algorithm for CT and MR images. Minz) to compress original raw files while preserving diagnostic quality. We also provide pre-generated DICOM versions of popular medical datasets, which can be easily integrated into existing workflows.

This study examines a class of $f(\mathcal{R})$ Lagrangian f(R) models that are both spherically symmetric and static, featuring a negative cosmological constant and a non-constant heat capacity. The analysis derives the mass and surface gravity of the black hole, allowing for a specific case where the mass and entropy satisfy the Bekenstein-Hawking formula and the mass-to-entropy ratio remains constant. Furthermore, it establishes that the black hole's entropy can be expressed as an entropy-area formula, with the latter being equivalent to an entropy-area formula derived within the framework of AdS/CFT duality.

We introduce a novel approach to unsupervised, fixed-length feature learning for long and flexible-length DNA sequences by applying a sequence-to-sequence autoencoder. This method first tokenizes sequences into a fixed set of $N$ elements, then trains a model to compress these inputs into a compressed, latent vector of $M$ features ($M<N$). This process enables the identification of the optimal latent dimension $M$, which reveals a specific, reusable representation of the data. We applied this framework to human and mouse germline sequences, discovering that the most effective representation emerges at $M=100$. Additionally, the text investigates scenarios where uniqueness is precluded by degeneracy, such as when optimal transport plans are not fully ranked and provides a methodology for reconstructing the underlying optimal transport plans in these unique-challenging cases.

This study examines the time-dependent behavior of a central degree of freedom interacting with a many-body localized (MBL) environment. We analyze the system using a one-dimensional Ising chain with quasi-disorder, which remains MBL even in its thermalizing phase, coupled to a central spin. We find that at zero temperature, the system exhibits both Rabi oscillations and many-body localized phenomena, whereas at finite temperatures, the interaction displays a fractal nature and anomalous diffusion. We also investigate how these effects are influenced by the interplay between different parameters.

Urban physical contacts and social networking are pivotal drivers of economic output and innovation. While the urban economics literature has extensively analyzed the economic value of city networking, it lacks a corresponding theoretical framework for the epidemiology of urban disease transmission. This paper bridges that gap by developing an epidemiological model for disease spread in urban settings, which incorporates the physical contact rate, the value of networking, and the optimal balance between the benefits of city life and its health risks. By integrating economic theory with established models from both epidemiology and urban economics, we derive a critical transmission threshold that is then empirically tested using data from the Chinese government's 2002 declaration of AIDS as a national epidemic. The test results indicate that the disease's spread in China is governed by this threshold, which is significantly influenced by the urban economics parameters of physical contact, the valuation of city life, and the effectiveness of preventive measures.

A two-step field-split nonlinear preconditioner is developed and evaluated for two-phase flow and transport challenges. This strategy decouples the highly nonlinear pressure equation from its significantly more linearly coupled concentration counterpart. Employing dual field splitting alongside linear preconditioning demonstrates superior robustness over dual time-stepping across various two-phase nonlinear scenarios. Specifically, the approach is applied to two-phase flow within heterogeneous vuggy carbonate reservoirs and multicomponent flow coupled with immiscible microscopic displacement processes featuring vortex source terms.

Distinguishing chiral enantiopes of chiral molecules via chiral light remains a highly active area of research. This study presents a theoretical investigation into a new scheme for generating chiral light by mixing a linearly polarized beam with a thermal radiation field within a Rydberg atomic medium. Because thermal radiation possesses no intrinsic chirality and the intrinsic hyperfine structure of ground-state Rydberg atoms renders the medium effectively chiral, the induced nonlinearity acts as a chiral filter. This interaction leads to different transmission coefficients for left- and right-handed circularly polarized components of an input probe beam, resulting in transmitted light that exhibits circular polarization and a measurable degree of elliptical polarization. This phenomenon offers a detection method for the ground-state hyperfine structure in Rydberg atoms and provides a controllable avenue for producing chiral photons.

This paper explores the role of boundary terms within two-dimensional string theory and Jackiw-Teilbary (JT) gravity. We demonstrate that these terms are essential for achieving consistent agreements between the amplitudes and actions in both the JT gravity framework and the two-dimensional string theory model. Furthermore, we show that these terms are critical for a coherent description of the duality in two-dimensional string theory, which mirrors the duality in the Witten model. These boundary terms also facilitate the extension of the Schwarzian action to the non-critical string theory of Jackiw-Teilbary. In the context of the stringy sigma model, we find a strong link between this action and the associated quantum wormhole physics. Finally, we discuss the implications for the wormy de Sitter space-time.

Urban infrastructure, such as pipelines and cables, was constructed without regard for future accessibility, rendering it difficult to repair or maintain without disruption once it begins to deteriorate. To prevent extensive service interruptions and environmental damage, a proactive strategy for locating and managing this underground asset is essential. However, the absence of a centralized, city-wide information system currently hinders such efforts. To address this gap, we introduce the concept of a "Digital Twin" for underground infrastructure. This proposal outlines the digital twin's architecture, which is designed to integrate data from diverse sources—including geospatial records, sensor data, and maintenance logs—into a single, cohesive framework. Ultimately, this system will empower urban planners to transition from reactive fixes to a forward-thinking approach to locating and sustaining underground assets.

We investigate the anisotropic spin dephasing of individual $^{171}$Yb$^+$ ions, which form a two-dimensional Wigner crystal suspended within a quadrupole trap. This spin dephasing stems from nuclear quadrupole interactions that are perturbed by transverse phonon modes. We establish that the associated dephasing time exhibits an anisotropic dependence on the excitation of the symmetric stretch and degenerate bending phonon modes. By correlating the dephasing dynamics with ions driven out of the flat equilibrium position, we demonstrate the control over this process through the adjustment of the applied plane laser field. Furthermore, we show that for specific bending phonon occupations, the dephasing time can be effectively extended.

Tip-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy (TERS) is a powerful imaging technique for analyzing molecular signatures within nanometer-scale volumes. This study employs finite-difference time-domain (FDT) simulations to evaluate a standard TERS geometry consisting of a sharp metallic conical probe positioned over a conductive substrate supporting a dielectric spacer and a single molecule. Simulations of the probe's near-field distribution are compared against the combined near-field and far-field contributions to a molecular cross-section, while surface plasmon polariton (SPP) modes are contrasted with these responses. We demonstrate that surface plasmons do not account for the significant near-field amplification observed at the probe tip, which drives the primary mechanisms of TERS signal enhancement. Instead, enhancement arises from the interplay of the probe's near-field and the combined near-field and far-field effects on the molecule, particularly at low dielectric spacer thicknesses. These findings are critical for optimizing experimental TERS designs to achieve maximum enhancement and minimal spatial resolution.

This study introduces a new 40 GHz dataset from the IRAM 30m telescope, which was previously utilized for the search for Anomalous Microwave Emission (AME) arising from the rotational excitation of interstellar dust. While no significant detection was made at that frequency, this work introduces a comprehensive calibration of the system using both non-radio and radio standards, alongside a detailed characterization of the antenna's primary sidelobe response. This advancement is expected to facilitate more sensitive future AME investigations.

Ammonium sulfate exhibits a unique triclinic cubic transition at ambient pressure that enables it to serve as a thermoelectric cooler and power generator. This study investigates the impact of chemical pressure induced by doping with organic salts on this phase transition. Specifically, we substitute small ammonium sulfate cations with larger ones from methyl- and dimethyl-tris(aminomethyl) salts. Our findings indicate that applying chemical pressure shifts the structural phase transition to higher pressures and suppresses the electronic second-order transitions that coincide with the structural shift. Consequently, these results offer insights into the pressure-driven behavior of similar compounds.

Probabilistic learning tasks often elicit either a maximization strategy, where agents select the most probable option, or a probability-matching strategy where responses are distributed in accordance with the underlying probabilities. While the conditions governing when agents adopt matching versus maximization are not fully understood, existing research has largely overlooked the role of the number of available choices. To address this, our study examined this variable using a novel automated framework where machines learn from the perspective of the agents they simulate. We tested these learners across scenarios involving one, two, or three options and discovered that both reinforcement learning models and humans exhibit a transition from maximization to probability matching as payoff structures become less extreme. This pattern holds for individuals and groups but is more pronounced in single people facing less extreme rewards matching. We further observed that while humans and learners alike become less consistent in their choices under less extreme conditions and strong temptation to match, they also adapt their strategies over time in response to how the environmental reward parameters shift.

This structure emerges from the local factors of what would be the root system for $E_8$ in any given theory. It is a known fact in mathematical physics and number theory that these forms are invariant under a specific transformation, and they are expected to play a significant role in the study of the root system for $E_8$ in any given theory.

This paper introduces a novel polyhedral structure, termed the Fréchet distance surface, designed to measure similarity between polygonal curves. This surface is constructed by plotting the Fréchet distance values across all pairs of parameters defining continuous curve deformations. While the exact computation of the Fréchet distance is known to be NP-hard, our proposed approach leverages the geometric properties of the distance function itself. This allows for the efficient generation of a geometric representation using a small number of vertices and facilitates the derivation of several new similarity metrics and corresponding optimization objectives. The validity and utility of this method are demonstrated through experiments on curve datasets and various machine learning use cases.

Measurement Error Mitigation (MEM) addresses systematic biases in quantum computing outcomes by applying classical post-processing techniques to data from repeated circuit executions. While MEM has been widely adopted for single-qubit $Y$-basis measurements, it lacks the necessary resources for large-scale mitigation on systems with many qubits. This limitation stems from MEM's reliance on extensive sampling to train probability distributions for every possible bit-flip pattern across all qubits, a process that becomes computationally prohibitive as qubit count increases. This paper introduces a new approach that significantly reduces the complexity of these probability distributions to model two-level systems instead of full multi-qubit states, rendering the task polynomial in complexity relative to the number of qubits. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method by applying it to MEM for multi-qubit $Z$-basis measurements on both IBM quantum processors and simulators. Our findings indicate that this efficient algorithm effectively handles random errors and provides a viable pathway for mitigating measurement errors on current and near-future Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) platforms.

Assisting humans with everyday tasks is a primary focus of robotics. In assistive teleoperation, where robots must interpret a human's intended action for a specific task, they can do so by monitoring the controller inputs associated with those intentions. To enhance assistance, robots should proactively learn their operators' control habits and use this knowledge to clarify their understanding. To achieve this, we introduce an online learning algorithm that simultaneously updates a robot's internal model of the physical environment and its model of the human controller. This algorithm relies on a predictive controller that leverages its environmental model to simulate the motion trajectories predicted from the robot's current state. By comparing the predictive controller's output with the actual human movements on the hardware, the system generates an error metric used to refine both the environmental model and the controller model through co-learning. Experimental results from a study involving six participants manipulating a robotic arm to stack objects demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness. When compared to a baseline random approach, our method achieved a statistically significant improvement in the percentage of correctly classified control actions, with findings of $94.4 \pm 2.1\%$ versus $68.3 \pm 10.1\%$ ($p < 0.001$).

At the heart of autonomous mobile robotics is the challenge of operating within unfamiliar environments. To address this, the paper introduces a new approach to simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) that leverages the concept of topological place recognition. By utilizing a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract and recognize places from LiDAR-based range images, the system generates an embedding for every image. These embeddings are then integrated into a robust place-based SLAM framework. This section details a novel place activation strategy designed to create a sparse, location-specific graph, which significantly enhances the efficiency of both computation and memory utilization. Experimental results from both simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves accurate place recognition and effective long-term consistency while maintaining high efficiency in both processing time and memory usage. Furthermore, the paper addresses the potential issue of place ambiguity in densely structured environments, such as corridors, by implementing a flexible probabilistic model that incorporates robot trajectory data to refine the weights of different recognized places.

The proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) has necessitated the creation of novel communication schemes capable of handling a vast array of heterogeneous devices. A critical requirement for future systems is the ability to transmit data using two-dimensional (2-D) arrangements, which has spurred the development of various 2-D array-based coding techniques. These methods are already in practical use within wireless IoT technologies like LoRa and ISM bands and face future integration with 5G and 6G networks. This paper introduces a universal framework for error correction tailored to heterogeneous 2-D array-based coding schemes. Additionally, a framework for automatically generating test patterns is proposed to facilitate the evaluation of existing and the design of new error correction methods. The effectiveness of the suggested approach is validated through simulations on standard LoRa configurations.

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively employed in medicine for diagnostics and treatment planning. While X-ray computed tomography (CT) is a widely used imaging technique that provides detailed information about the internal structure of an object, it is not without limitations. One limitation is that polyenergetic X-ray sources introduce artefacts that can affect image quality. Additionally, although single-energy sources are often used to avoid these issues, they have a lower contrast-to-noise ratio compared to polyenergetic sources. To address these limitations, this study proposes a data-driven approach that combines the benefits of both single-energy and polyenergetic sources. This approach uses machine learning algorithms to process data from both types of sources and generate an image that is free from artefacts while maintaining a high contrast-to-noise ratio. The proposed data-driven approach is evaluated on a real dataset from a medical CT scanner. This study demonstrates that the proposed data-driven approach is effective in improving image quality by reducing artefacts and maintaining a high contrast-to-noise ratio. The results indicate that the proposed data-driven approach is comparable to or better than traditional image processing methods in terms of image quality. This study has implications for future research in the field of image processing and machine learning.

This work investigates the propagation of light within a metallic area covered by a thin dielectric film, comparing a local response framework with a hydrodynamic approach for electrons. We establish that while both methods yield consistent results in insulating materials regarding optical properties, the local response model frequently produces field divergences within metals due to an unphysical inversion of signs in the metal's dielectric function. In contrast, the hydrodynamic model remains finite and physically realistic even when these divergences appear in nearby dielectrics. Consequently, we conclude from several metallic-dielectric interfaces analyzed that the hydrodynamic model is necessary for an accurate representation of metals in macroscopic periodic structures operating in reflection or transmission modes.

Although information retrieval systems have advanced, users often overlook the significant potential of their own contexts. We introduce the concept of User Context Retrieval (UCR), a framework where users actively select specific aspects of their context to assist in subsequent retrieval tasks. We posit that since users are uniquely positioned to identify which contextual elements are most pertinent and meaningful, their input will surpass automated extraction methods (such as sensors or voice assistants) in assisting with subsequent search. To this end, we developed a user study evaluating the effectiveness of active context provision by ordinary people. The results demonstrate a substantial boost in IR performance when individuals explicitly contribute contextual data, with identification of high-performing user-provided context leading to a 10-fold improvement in IR outcomes.

This work introduces a forecasting method designed to capture key temporal series attributes, including stationarity, periodicity, and potential structural breaks. Multivariate time series data are initially converted into a set of features and a forecast function. Features are generated using a learned model, while feature selection is performed via a model-based approach. Empirical evidence from simulations and real-world experiments demonstrates that this method outperforms existing techniques in these areas.

Artificial intelligence-driven Machine Learning (ML) techniques have become a vital asset in modern healthcare, particularly in leveraging digital health records (EHRs) to enhance care quality through data analysis. These ML models facilitate various applications, including disease prediction, diagnosis, drug discovery, and care planning. However, current research predominantly relies on tabular data, largely ignoring the richness of unstructured text within clinical notes. Although Natural Language Processing (NLP) has advanced significantly in recent years, its application in healthcare remains constrained by scarce high-quality datasets. Consequently, this study introduces a new approach to disease prediction that utilizes state-of-the-art NLP models to process unstructured clinical text. Specifically, it employs pre-trained BERT architectures to extract features from unstructured clinical notes and applies a Random Forest classifier for effective and efficient disease detection.

This study employs density functional theory to examine how solvent properties influence the behavior of dilute electrolyte solutions in contact with charged surfaces. We evaluate the impact of the solvent's dielectric profile on mean-field predictions, presenting a novel DFT framework that accounts for the dynamic coupling between ionic density and solvent polarization. This approach includes a Pekar-type energy term to model local solvent polarization induced by an electric field. We demonstrate that dielectric polarization significantly alters the electrostatic potential and the statistical distribution of ions, a factor that becomes especially critical when dealing with low-dielectric solvents or substantial dielectric mismatches between the solvent and a nearby surface.

Automating the identification of requirements from textual data is a critical initial step in numerous natural language processing applications. However, existing automated techniques are often restricted to processing structured input, while others rely on automated identification methods that are either limited in their scope or lack the ability to accurately capture necessary details. To address these limitations, we introduce a new algorithm that extracts requirements from unstructured text. This system leverages language models to extract requirements directly, without relying on manual intervention. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first algorithm capable of accurately extracting requirements from completely unstructured text. We evaluated the system using a dataset of 1,000 documents and found that it achieved an F1 score of 0.85.

This study examines the energy efficiency (EE) of a maximum diversity network coding (MDNC) scheme designed to mitigate the "energy per bit" challenge. In systems employing MDNC, data packets are transmitted from multiple sources to a central sink, which then aggregates and forwards the combined data to a single destination. We introduce a mathematical framework to calculate the end-to-end energy efficiency (EE) for both scenarios: one incorporating network coding and one excluding it. To determine the optimal transmission power that maximizes EE, we derived a closed-form solution using the third-order Lambert W function. Simulation results demonstrate that the EE in a network coding-enabled scenario surpasses that of a non-coding scenario. Furthermore, we found that raising the source count further enhances EE within the network coding context.

We introduce a model to examine how local order parameters are perturbed near magnetic impurities positioned on a superconducting surface. By employing a theoretical framework grounded in surface Green's functions and a self-consistent, local version of the anomalous gap equation, we analyze these changes numerically. These findings are compared against YSR states associated with magnetic impurities embedded in a BCS superconductor. The comparison reveals that local order parameter depressions are significantly more severe in systems with surface impurities than those with impurities bulk-located. This difference stems from anisotropic properties in both the order parameter and YSR states for impurities on surfaces.

Distribution-to-distribution registration methods are widely used for point cloud registration, yet they struggle with heavy occlusions and scene dynamics, as their static nature prevents handling displacement caused by movement. This work introduces a new approach designed to align point clouds within dynamic environments. This method begins by establishing a correspondence between the centroids of two distributions, followed by registering corresponding rings around those centroids. Subsequent correspondences are iteratively determined for further outer rings until the entire scene is registered. To ensure robustness, the registration process for each ring incorporates RANSAC to filter outliers. The validity of this method is confirmed through evaluation on open access datasets, with results demonstrating an accuracy of 98.24% on the DynamicScene dataset and an IoU of 86.91% on the SemanticKITTI benchmark.

Satellite imagery is widely used across diverse sectors such as agriculture, city planning, and the monitoring of natural disasters. However, the sheer volume of images generated daily makes it nearly impossible for humans to keep up with analysis demands. While current approaches often rely on pre-defined, rigid models that struggle to handle the wide variety of image types, this paper introduces a new framework leveraging large language models (LLMs) to interpret satellite data. Unlike traditional methods, our proposed system utilizes an LLM-driven agent capable of dynamically adapting to varying image domains through few-shot learning. Additionally, the system incorporates an observational agent equipped with Large Multimodal Models (LMMs), which interprets image content to communicate effectively with the LLM agent. We validate the efficacy of this dual-agent architecture across three distinct satellite imagery datasets, demonstrating its robust performance in varying conditions.

Non-linear X-ray Absorption Near Edge Spectroscopy (XANES) is a technique used to observe radiation-induced structural changes in matter at an atomic level, operating within a regime where absorbed photon flux is sufficient to alter material properties on a timescale comparable to the experimental measurement. In this work, we present findings from non-linear XANES experiments conducted on water, analyzing variations in spectral features as functions of both incident fluence and temporal delay. The study reveals a shift in the peak position and reduction in spectral intensity that scales with fluence. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the depolarization of incident light is a critical factor influencing these fluence-dependent spectral modifications. Finally, we provide a detailed examination of the potential contributions from photoionization, knock-on electron effects, and the depolarization of sample alignment to these observed phenomena.

Modulation classification (MC) is a vital component of cognitive radio systems, enabling receivers to identify the signal type and facilitating automatic message handling. Although recent Deep Neural Network (DNN) approaches have demonstrated high MC accuracy, they often demand substantial computational resources, resulting in significant power consumption. This study introduces a novel DNN-based MC method that leverizes the inherent characteristics of a specific constellation to achieve both high precision and low power usage. Furthermore, the proposed architecture supports a multi-task framework that can be extended to handle multiple modulation schemes.

Segmenting MS lesions in MRI presents a significant challenge for conventional deep learning approaches because the vast number of normal-appearing brain structures can be mistaken for lesions. This study introduces a new method utilizing a multi-structure transformer, an architecture designed to mitigate the risk of false predictions by integrating long-range contextual information. We evaluated this method across two distinct datasets: a public dataset containing 210 MRI scans and a private dataset with 220 scans. The results demonstrate that our new transformer approach outperforms established models, including U-Net, ResUNet, PointPillor, and other transformer architectures, on both datasets.

The authors demonstrate a non-rigid approach to the closed loop condition (also known as the closed loop condition or closed loop criterion) within optimal transport theory on Riemannian manifolds. They provide a simplified proof of the closed loop condition derived by Amadori, Gigli, and Gigli, and through the application of this non-rigid framework, they derive an alternative and simplified proof of Torii-McKean-Wang condition utilizing closed loop criteria and related concepts.

This work addresses the issue of learning from ergodic continuous-time systems, where the objective is to construct a model that accurately represents the true dynamics. We demonstrate that by reducing the generalization error to a vanishingly small level, one can only requires a sufficiently long observation window $T$ to grow exponentially with the dimension of the continuous state. Furthermore, we show that the generalization error can be expressed as the square of the $L^2$ distance between the actual and estimated transition probabilities. Finally, the methodology is demonstrated through an application to stochastic differential equations.

We conducted millimeter-wave continuum observations of the infrared dark cloud (IRDC) G029.26+00.21 at 1.3 mm using the ALMA to investigate star-forming cores within the dense molecular ridge. Our data reveal 19 cores, 17 of which are associated with detected protostars. By analyzing the velocity structure, we identified three distinct outflow positions at approximately 11 km s$^{-1}$, 21 km s$^{-1}$, and 29 km s$^{-1}$, indicating multiple outflows along the same line of sight. The 19 detected cores are spatially distributed into two groups separated by a low-density region roughly 1.5 pc in length. The group located at lower velocities contains 19 starless cores and 19 protostellar cores. In contrast, the group at higher velocities comprises 18 starless cores and 19 protostellar cores. The study reveals that protostellar cores are consistently more massive than their starless counterparts in both velocity groups, suggesting that star formation preferentially occurs in denser, more massive regions.

Primordial black holes (PBHs) are hypothesized to be a component of dark matter. This study explores the PBH dark matter scenario specifically regarding dwarf spheroidal galaxies (dSphs). We examine three distinct methods for isolating dSpheroidal galaxies from the Milky Way's satellite system: by distance, by mass, and by velocity dispersion. The analysis of these systems indicates that they are subject to mass loss, which can be attributed to dynamical friction, tidal stripping, or evaporation. We then evaluate the constraints on dark matter fractions within dSpheroidal galaxies by contrasting theoretical predictions with observed data, utilizing a binary black hole deconvolution model. Our results suggest an upper limit on the dark matter fraction of 80% for M20, 70% for Segue 1, and 50% for Segue 2.

This work employs molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the liquid crystalline phases of wedge-shaped, monodisperse molecules, analyzing how they respond to wedge angles and packing density. We analyze the transition between isotropic and nematic phases as a function of the wedge angle and packing density, finding that the wedge shape induces liquid crystalline phases beyond the standard isotropic-nematic transition. Specifically, packing densities below 0.5 yield liquid crystalline phases characterized by nematic order and additional suborientational symmetries, such as bi- and tri-uni axial order, which are highly responsive to the wedge angle. Conversely, the system exhibits a weak dependence of its bi- and tri-axial order on the wedge angle when the packing density exceeds 0.5. Furthermore, at packing densities above this threshold, the system undergoes a transition from bi- to tri-uni axial order, which is strongly influenced by the wedge angle. These findings demonstrate that the packing density of wedge-shaped molecules critically governs their liquid crystalline phases.

Parameter-efficient tuning focuses on updating a restricted portion of parameters when applying deep learning models to specific tasks. This approach is widely adopted in natural language processing, particularly with pre-trained models like BERT, which are adapted using methods such as Adapter layers, LoD, and Prompt tuning. Despite these variations, existing techniques often struggle with a trade-off between performance and resource usage, failing to fully leverage the benefits of efficiency. This paper introduces a new method called "AXA" (or similar acronym expansion) that addresses this issue effectively by utilizing axial attention mechanisms and adaptive analysis strategies tailored for BERT adaptation. The axial attention mechanism operates by combining horizontal and vertical axis information, reducing the overall complexity while maintaining performance comparable to full attention. Additionally, the proposed adaptive analysis strategy selectively refines the model based on input characteristics, enhancing performance without requiring full parameter adjustment. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that AXA achieves performance comparable to full fine-tuning while significantly reducing memory usage during both training and inference phases.

This paper introduces a memory-efficient, multi-layer perceptron-based comparison architecture that utilizes a pointer-based representation of dynamic memory. It effectively processes the "next" (pointer to following element) and "data" (actual value stored) fields to perform set addition via sampling, then evaluates the network's ability to identify two nearly identical sets differing by only single inserted items, with experimental results confirming a high degree of accuracy in these two-scenario tests.

This study examines the interconnections among the internal energy, enthalpy, and configurational entropy of polymer fluids. We establish the correlation between these forms of energy and configurational entropy, as well as link them through the thermodynamic derivative \(\partial U/\partial T = T\partial U/\partial T + a(T)\), where \(a(T)\) is a function independent of polymerization degree for the class of fluids considered. Furthermore, the analysis incorporates the thermodynamic theory of regular solutions, leading to a generalized Lennard-Jones potential that accounts for configurational interactions. This work extends the foundational theory regarding the internal energy, enthalpy, and configurational entropy of polymer fluids, providing an alternative perspective to complement the findings of Doi and Edwards.

It is widely acknowledged that even advanced transformer-based language models struggle with simple logical reasoning tasks involving negation. Specifically, models often fail to identify statements that are contrary to what they know, or that imply a previous statement. To address this gap, we introduce a series of methods to better evaluate how models handle negation, along a corresponding dataset. Our findings indicate that while these models have established baselines for such tasks, they lack the capability to dynamically apply operators like 'not' based on contextual parameters. Furthermore, experiments with interventions suggest that mere token masking is insufficient to trigger this operator behavior. Instead, models appear to require explicit symbolic grounding for operators to function correctly.

Real-time generation of new terms by neural machine translation (NMT) relies on both the source input and previously generated outputs, though this dependency on earlier words is not yet fully understood. This study investigates such generation patterns in phrase-based and sequence-based NMT models. First, we demonstrate that generated phrases are strongly dependent on specific source phrases, occurring with a frequency and distribution that closely mirror those of the original. Furthermore, we reveal that generated tokens are significantly dependent on both context and preceding generated tokens. Building on these findings, we propose a straightforward and efficient training method that incorporates the dependency on prior generated outputs to significantly boost translation performance. These experiments were conducted using the MNIST multilingual corpus, a multilingual version of MNIST that translates text across multiple languages.

This work introduces a collection of identities regarding the weights of curvature graphs within a symplectic manifold, including explicit formulations for curvature-specific and variationally linked curvature graphs by employing both standard commutators and Lie curvature commutators. As a result, we derive simplified expressions for weights specific to curvature on symplectic spheres and minimal weight criteria for curvature graphs. The authors also establish two distinct commutative properties of curvature graphs. Building on these properties, we establish a commutative form of Arvanitoyeorgos's combinatorial inequality. Furthermore, we present new, sharper combinatorial bounds that are more restrictive than Arvanitoyeorgos's original version, specifically in cases where the first and third eigenvalues of the Hessian of the function $f$ share the same sign. Accurately determining camera poses is fundamental for camera calibration and coordinate system localization within image-based robotic systems. While classical methods like PnP, EPnP, and SAMP rely on feature points for pose estimation, these methods are often restricted by issues related to computational efficiency, robustness, and robustness. The investigation of complex networks is vital for understanding natural phenomena and technological systems. A central aspect of this field involves analyzing its structural components, particularly the identification of fully-weighted clusters, which are defined as maximal subgraphs where all edges possess non-zero values compared to hybrid methods. Existing algorithms for detecting these fully-weighted clusters typically rely on a branch-and-bound approach, relying heavily on the selection of a bounding function to filter out infeasible candidates. However, current approaches often fail to fully leverage edge weights during this process. This paper introduces a new framework that combines fully-weighted clustering concepts with clique-based search strategies, specifically designed to handle the challenges posed by weighted edges. By doing so, our method significantly accelerates the identification of both the largest and heaviest cliques within complex networks. Furthermore, it demonstrates superior performance in enumerating all maximal cliques and identifying fully-weighted clusters, surpassing the capabilities of traditional hybrid approaches.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have garnered significant attention for modeling complex systems by integrating physical system characteristics into a data-driven architecture. While purely data-specific models often struggle with robustness and generalization when encountering unseen scenarios, PINNs embed prior domain knowledge to enhance these capabilities. This work introduces a methodology for constructing PINNs that incorporate graph-based representations of systems. Specifically, graph convolutional networks are utilized to teach neurons spatial and relational domain knowledge. We validate the approach on problems involving partial differential equations and the 3D structure prediction of proteins. Results demonstrate that this graph-based PINN outperforms standard fully connected networks in terms of sample efficiency and robustness.

Air pollution monitoring stations are often sparsely distributed, which hinders the precise modeling of exposure in epidemiological studies. We propose a new method that integrates geographic information systems (GIS) and machine learning to enhance this exposure modeling. Using California's epidemiological cohort as a case study, we applied a random forest algorithm to predict air pollution levels by incorporating data on land use, road networks, and proximity to air quality sensors. Consequently, this approach significantly improved the modeling of short-term air pollution exposure for California residents.

We present the first experimental verification of a Majorana zero-energy state in the zero-bias peak of a gold/superconducting nanowire junction. The device, consisting of a gold segment coupled to a 6 nm indium-antimony (InAs) superconducting nanowire via a tunnel junction, was fabricated using standard techniques. Our findings reveal that the Majorana peak is sensitive to both thermal variations and adjustments in the bias voltage. Specifically in terms of temperature, the peak diminishes gradually as $T$ rises and recovers as it falls, with a characteristic scale of approximately 0.5 K. Furthermore, introducing bias voltage in the range of 0.00 to 0.00 A results in a significant reduction of the Majorana peak, which recovers at higher values. These observations, combined with a standard one-dimensional model for the system, provide a comprehensive description of the observed tunneling conductance behavior. Collectively, the results support the presence of a Majorana zero-energy state in the gold/InAs superconducting heterostructure.

This research investigates the eigenvalues of design matrices arising in linear bandit settings with "nice" action sets to enhance our understanding of online learning dynamics. We demonstrate that the spectrum dictates anticipated cumulative regret for numerous standard linear bandit algorithms. Furthermore, we show that the cumulative regret of a diverse range of methods can be bounded through the Riemannian trace norm of the matrix, which is derived from its eigenvalues. This framework enables a unified analysis of several prevalent action environments, including the unit ball, hypercube, and simplicion constraints. We also address the theoretical boundaries of this approach, showing that the cumulative regret cannot always be fully determined by the eigenvalues. These results offer a more robust foundation for analyzing online linear learning mechanisms.

Gapped graphene, which exhibits a non-zero band gap, displays a quantized orbital Hall effect (OHE) driven by the finite orbital magnetic moments of its band edges. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of both the OHE and orbital anomalous Hall effect (OAE) within this system. We demonstrate that whenever a bulk physical quantity is present, it dictates specific surface and edge phenomena; specifically, the bulk Berry curvature acts as the key determinant of the OHE, while the surface Hall conductivity and edge Hall conductance arise directly from corresponding bulk and edge characteristics. Furthermore, it is shown that a surface Hall conductivity of $-e\mathcal{A}_{\text{surf}}/2\pi\sigma$ and edge Hall conductance of $-e\mathcal{A}_{\text{surf}}\sigma/\pi$ are governed by surface and edge Anomalous Nernst effects, respectively. These findings are validated through explicit calculations of the OHE, OAE, surface Hall, edge transport, Surface Nernst effect (SNE), and edge Nernst effect (ENE) using a tight-binding model.

While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved significant success in handling irregular data through the graph classification task, they remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks that introduce subtle perturbations to node features, thereby degrading model performance. To address this, we introduce a new training approach leveraging the node features of graphs to enhance model robustness. Specifically, we propose the Node Feature Adversarial Training (NFAT) framework, which operates by applying gradient-based methods to generate node-level adversarial masks. These masks strategically mask features to maximize loss increase, with these generated masks then incorporated into the training process to bolster attack resistance. Comprehensive testing on standard benchmarks reveals that our method remains highly effective despite severe feature masking attacks, outperforming current state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, an extensive empirical analysis explores how critical hyperparameters, such as the proportion of masked features in mask generation, influence model performance.

This study employs non-equilibrium statistical mechanics to examine the Soret effect in binary systems composed of dimers and monomers within a thermal gradient. We specifically address the issue of calculating the thermal diffusion factor $\alpha$, which is an integral component of the Soret coefficient. To achieve this, we derive the collisional contribution to the energy-flux equation using collision expansion techniques, thereby extending the traditional Boltzmann equation framework. By applying the newly developed binary-mixture collision model alongside the recently proposed binary-mixture collision expansion method, we calculate thermal diffusion factor $\alpha$ as a function of the reduced temperature. We further analyze how the thermal diffusion factor $\alpha$ is influenced by the binary mixture's parameters.

Automated Essay Scoring (AES) demands a nuanced blend of linguistic proficiency and domain-specific knowledge to attain high accuracy. While the field has seen substantial progress in the last decade, the majority of recent research has prioritized surface-level linguistic features rather than deep semantic content. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes a novel, attention-driven framework designed to enhance both linguistic and semantic accuracy in AES tasks. Additionally, the study includes a new, publicly available dataset that combines rich linguistic annotations with ground-trust scores. Experimental results demonstrate that the suggested model significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art performance in automated scoring.

A critical challenge in adapting domains for pedestrian detection lies in the severe disparity in lighting conditions between domains, which significantly impacts detection precision. Although many current approaches attempt light invariant feature alignment by inverting the conventional method—first inverting images before applying domain adaptation—there remains a risk that this ignores important lighting cues. To address this, we introduce a novel approach called LABAug, a novel light-specific data augmentation technique. LABAug operates in LabColor space to vary illumination intensities, directions, and hues, thereby creating illumination-diverse pedestrian datasets. This diverse training data enables detectors to learn light-invariant features more effectively. Comprehensive experiments on three pedestrian datasets demonstrate that LABAug consistently surpasses state-of-the-lighting benchmarks, demonstrating an improvement of up to 10.4% in detection accuracy.

This study introduces a new method for identifying deviations from optimal movement patterns in overarm throwing actions. While previous research has relied on visual models and expert knowledge to label motion capture datasets, this work proposes a novel framework employing a multi-modal neural network to simultaneously infer the Point of Release (PoR) timing and throw direction. Unlike manual labeling, our approach requires no pre-existing data annotations. Experimental throw results indicate that PoR estimations achieve an average error margin below 2 cm. Furthermore, our system effectively identifies sub-optimal throwing techniques; notably, it correctly flagged errors in overhand high-style and side-chest-style deliveries, which involve normal variations in throwing mechanics. In contrast, the model struggled to detect errors in an underhand-style overhead delivery. This suggests that for PoR-based error identification to remain robust across diverse datasets, the training set must encompass a broad spectrum of throwing actions.

This study introduces a straightforward approach to incorporating syntactic information into Neural Machine Translation (NMT) by utilizing the output from a tree-linear decoder to build a structural attention matrix based on the parse trees of source sentences. This structural attention matrix is concatenated with a standard sequence-based matrix to serve as input for a multi-level decoder. This hybrid attention mechanism acts as an effective shortcut for internalizing syntactic data, enabling the model to function more robustly as an NMT system. Specifically, this hybrid attention significantly boosts performance in low-resource settings and consistently improves performance across various languages in standard scenarios. Furthermore, testing on ten languages demonstrates that structural attention derived from both dependency and constituent parsing vastly outperforms that from dependency parsing alone, establishing that constituent parsing is superior to dependency parsing for syntactic augmentation in NMT applications.

Accurate modeling of astrochemical processes relies heavily on precise binding energy values. However, current models often employ approximate energies derived from a limited set of laboratory experiments, resulting in minimal variability across different data sets and negligible impact on predicted abundances. In this study, the binding energies for H₂CO and HCN on a water substrate are analyzed by incorporating random variations in individual training parameters within a Machine Learning framework. These perturbations generate multiple simulations to assess their effect on the abundance of every modeled species across various interstellar conditions, including cold molecular clouds, warm molecular clouds, and protoplanetary disks. The resulting models reveal significant sensitivity to the training data; specifically, the abundance of 20 species exhibits a marked difference between the extreme limits of simulated scenarios. Furthermore, the study identifies H₂CO and HCN abundances as particularly sensitive to these variations. This outcome indicates an intrinsic limitation in current modeling approaches and suggests an urgent need for broader experimental binding energy data to improve predictive accuracy.

This study examines a multiplicative stochastic process characterized by reflection at a logarithmic lower bound following a Rayleigh distribution, while the upper tail extends indefinitely. This research is a continuation of work by Bouchaud and Jeulin, who established the process's stationary probability density (pd) as a Stieltjes convolution of two specific components. Building on this foundation, our paper demonstrates that these two components can be expressed in terms of Hermite and Bessel functions, respectively. Consequently, the stationary pd emerges as a series representation involving Hermite polynomials with coefficients determined by Bessel functions. Furthermore, we derive a practical approximation for this density and validate it against computer simulations.

We introduce an efficient approach for the compressed tomography of large entangled quantum states, leveraging their inherent structure to drastically reduce the number of required measurements. Our method utilizes random measurements on $k$ auxiliary systems to construct an effective mixed state that exhibits structural depth, which we refer to as a depth-effective state. By showing that this state is structurally equivalent to the original system's density matrix, we demonstrate that its depth can be exploited for efficient tomographic reconstruction. Specifically, we show that the computational cost of reconstructing a general quantum state scales linearly with its depth. This relationship is further supported by TomoRecon simulations, which validate the accuracy and efficiency of our approach.

Deep learning models for machine learning often face challenges due to insufficient training data, particularly in medical contexts where expert annotation is scarce and costly. This study addresses these limitations by evaluating image augmentation strategies to enhance the performance of semantic segmentation networks using a limited dataset of labeled chest X-rays for pneumonia detection. The research compares three augmentation methods—Data Augmentation, Auto Data Augmentation (ADA), and Progressive Neural Process Modeling (PNP)—to determine their efficacy in minimizing reliance on labeled data. Results indicate that while all methods improve performance over a baseline trained on fewer labels, the simplest Data Augmentation approach achieved the best performance on the pneumonia classification task with the fewest number of labeled images, outperforming more sophisticated techniques like ADA and PN P in that specific context.

While state-of-the-art image captioning models produce grammatically correct and content-rich descriptions, they typically lack control over specific narrative attributes like style or target audience. This study introduces a straightforward yet powerful approach to create such a controlled capability. By training the decoder with a mixture of synthetic caption batches—constructed by applying random transformations to existing data during training—we enable the generation of captions tailored to specified traits defined in input text. For instance, this allows for distinct outputs ranging from "film critic" reviews to "emojis," or shifting a basic caption from "a person on a beach" to a "nostalgic" description of "someone enjoying a sunny beach day." The proposed method requires only a single pass of training and can be seamlessly integrated into any existing image captioning architecture by modifying the data sampling strategy during that training phase. Experimental results on the Flickr30k dataset demonstrate that the model effectively learns both explicit and implicit task constraints from textual inputs while maintaining or improving overall performance compared to previous methods.

The proliferation of autonomous systems and decision-making algorithms has intensified the necessity to define "harm" to guide research and development toward public benefit. This paper proposes a novel framework for defining harm that leverages the insights from causal modeling. Utilizing causal models, we formulate harm as the capacity to alter outcomes negatively for specific demographic groups. This demographic-centric approach clarifies how harm can be demonstrated system-wide, for individual entities, and through specific design choices. Furthermore, the associated analytical tools demonstrate that demonstrating harm is directly contingent upon establishing causal links between an autonomous system and adverse outcomes for particular groups. Consequently, the proposed definition facilitates the operationalization of the goal to prevent all such systems from producing negative impacts on specific demographic groups.
